notes:
I've put together notes for most of the chapter. A few things to know first:

- **Missing verses.** The fullest verse-by-verse source, Enduring Word, came through cut off after v. 12. For vv. 13–33 I only saw its summary lines, and I found nothing at all on vv. 16 and 30–31.
- **No Catholic, Orthodox or prosperity sources.** I found no pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org, and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching. Catholic material below comes only from translations and Clarke's reports of them. So the brief's third section is thin: only some modern-scholarship notes on v. 1 and v. 6.
- **Denomination labels are mine.** The pages didn't state them. I'm calling Adam Clarke Methodist, John Gill and Spurgeon Baptist, and Matthew Henry Presbyterian/Nonconformist. Please check these before printing.

---

**v. 1**
- **Who Agur was.** Guzik says Agur is known only from this chapter, and that the "men of Hezekiah" added his words when they gathered more material (Prov 25:1). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **Not Solomon.** Clarke reports that some take Agur to be Solomon and Jakeh to be David, with Ithiel and Ucal as titles of Christ. He thinks they were real people about whom we know nothing more. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-30.html
- **Teacher and students.** Clarke thinks Agur was a public teacher and Ithiel and Ucal his students. He reads *massa* ("oracle") as a message given by the Holy Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-30.html
- **Ithiel and Ucal as Messiah?** Guzik notes that Trapp saw the two names as hidden references to the Messiah. Guzik thinks this unlikely and quotes Poole asking why such obscure names would be used. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **Gill.** Gill reports a view that the two names are titles of God himself ("God with me" and "the mighty One"), whom Agur is addressing. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/proverbs/30-1.html
- **Weariness leads to dependence.** Bible Hub's study notes say Agur's weariness does not end in despair. It prepares the way for depending on the Lord. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/30-1.htm
- **Modern scholarship.** The NET notes say there have been many attempts to reinterpret vv. 1–2. The Greek version translated "Ithiel" and "Ukal" instead of treating them as names, giving "I am weary, O God, I am weary and faint." The NRSV and NLT follow that approach. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Pro+30%3A1%3B31%3A1
- **The BSB's own footnote.** It offers "I am weary, O God, but I can prevail" by re-reading the vowels; the Hebrew as printed reads "to Ithiel and Ucal." https://www.biblehub.com/app/proverbs-30.htm
- **Massa as a place.** The Pulpit Commentary reports a view that *massa* is not "oracle" but a land of Massa, named after a son of Ishmael (Gen 25:14). Its people were among the "children of the East" known for wisdom. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/30-1.htm
- **Catholic rendering.** The Douay-Rheims, translated from the Latin Vulgate, treats the names as ordinary words: "The words of Gatherer the son of Vomiter." https://biblehub.com/proverbs/30-1.htm

**vv. 2–3**
- **Humility.** Guzik says Agur is using poetic exaggeration about his limits. He links it to a theme across Proverbs: humility is essential to wisdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **Spurgeon.** Spurgeon thinks Agur meant what he said. He suggests Agur felt this way after the Spirit had enlightened him: because God had taught him much, he felt he knew little. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/proverbs-30.html
- **Applying it.** Spurgeon says feeling inferior should keep no one from trusting God or serving him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/proverbs-30.html
- **Clarke.** Clarke says these words could not be true of Solomon. He thinks Agur may have been an uneducated countryman, like Amos, who knew what he knew by inspiration. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-30.html

**v. 4**
- **The answer is God.** Guzik says the passage sounds like Job 38–39, and the humble answer to each question is "God, and not man." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **God's name.** Guzik says we can know God's name, meaning his nature and character, only by God's own revelation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **Rhetorical questions.** TGC (Alex Kirk) compares the questions to God answering Job from the whirlwind. The only answer is Yahweh. Kirk suggests Jesus may be alluding to this verse in John 3:13, revealing himself as the answer to the mystery. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/agur-proverbs-30/
- **Where the traditions differ: "his Son's name."**
  - *Gill (Baptist):* the verse refers to a Son with the same nature as God, existing alongside him, equal to him, yet a distinct person. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/30-4.html
  - *Matthew Henry (Presbyterian/Nonconformist):* the verse points ahead to the One who came down from heaven and went back up. The Messiah is a person distinct from the Father, though his name was still secret. https://biblehub.com/par/proverbs/30-4.htm
  - *Clarke (Methodist):* he grants that many see the first and second persons of the Trinity here. He warns against resting that doctrine on so obscure a text: "Quote nothing that is not clear." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-30.html
  - *Barnes:* the first point is that humans cannot tell whether human relationships like fatherhood apply to God at all. If there is an Only-begotten, he is as beyond us as the Father until revealed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/30-4.html
  - *Guzik (Calvary Chapel, charismatic-leaning):* we do not know how far Agur foresaw the Messiah, but Agur knew God had a Son. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **Other readings of "Son."** GotQuestions says Agur may have had Israel in mind as God's son, or the personified Wisdom of Prov 8. Only looking back can New Testament readers be sure the name is Jesus. https://www.gotquestions.org/what-is-the-name-of-His-son.html
- **Wisdom or Logos.** The Pulpit Commentary says some Greek manuscripts read "his children," as if meaning Israel, but rejects this. It suggests Wisdom (Prov 8:22) or a Logos-type idea as possible answers. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/30-4.htm

**v. 5**
- **Purified like metal.** Clarke says "pure" is a picture taken from refining metal: God's word has no error mixed in. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-30.html
- **Trust, not bare knowledge.** Guzik, quoting Kidner, says revelation aims to build trust in the Speaker, not just knowledge. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **Inerrancy.** GotQuestions takes the verse to show that Scripture in its original form is without error. https://www.gotquestions.org/every-word-of-God-is-pure.html

**v. 6**
- **Over-interpreting.** Guzik, quoting Garrett, applies the warning to teachers who find more in a passage than is really there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **Equal authority.** Matthew Henry says it forbids putting anything beside God's word as equal in authority, even if it is offered as an explanation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/30-6.html
- **Traditions.** The Pulpit Commentary applies the warning to human traditions and rabbinic glosses. https://biblehub.com/proverbs/30-6.htm
- **Protestant vs Catholic.** Clarke uses this verse openly against the Roman Catholic Church. He says it added the Apocrypha, legends and traditions to God's word. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-30.html I found no Catholic reply on the permitted sites.
- **Original meaning.** Keil and Delitzsch link the verse to Deut 4:2. They take "his words" to mean God's self-revelation to Israel recorded in the Torah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/30-6.htm
- **NET note.** The Hebrew verb means "shown to be false," so anyone who adds to or changes God's word will be seen as a liar. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Pro&chapter=30&verse=6

**vv. 7–9**
- **For God's glory.** Guzik says Agur fears both extremes because either could make him profane God's name. He quotes Waltke: God's glory, not Agur's need, drives the prayer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **What the "lies" are.** Garrett, quoted by Guzik, takes the "falsehood and lies" to be the false promises of wealth and of poverty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **Clarke: idolatry.** Clarke is convinced the Hebrew words for "vanity" and "lies" point to idols. He reads the first request as a prayer against false religion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-30.html
- **Gill: sin in general.** Gill reads the first request as a prayer to be kept from sin, which is deceitful. He calls the middle condition the happiest and least tempted. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/proverbs/30-8.html
- **Concern for God's honour.** Matthew Henry says Agur fears stealing not because of the punishment but because it would dishonour God and discredit his faith. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_030.cfm
- **Lawful to pray for daily needs.** Older sermons collected on Bible Hub (Witherspoon) say it is right to pray for earthly blessings. Beddome calls this a prayer of preference rather than an absolute ban on riches. https://biblehub.com/sermons/proverbs/30-8.htm

**v. 10**
- **Slander.** Guzik reads this as harsh, unfair criticism of someone who is not present. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **Kidner.** Quoted by Guzik: if the servant is innocent, his curse will count, because there is a Judge. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/

**vv. 11–14**
- **Four evils.** Clarke lists them as mistreating parents, self-righteousness, pride, and cruelly oppressing the poor. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-30.html
- **Self-righteousness.** Guzik says a generation blind to its own sin will never be washed. He quotes Waltke linking this to the self-righteous Pharisees. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **Mockery.** Kirk (TGC) reads vv. 11–15 as deliberately shocking mockery of proud, greedy youth who exploit the weak. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/agur-proverbs-30/

**v. 15**
- **Leech and daughters.** Clarke reports Calmet's reading: the leech is covetousness, and its two daughters are avarice and ambition. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-30.html
- **Clarke's own guess.** He suggests "Alukah" may be the personal name of a well-known woman with two notoriously greedy daughters. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-30.html
- **Guzik.** He links vv. 15b–16 to the greedy generation just described. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/

**v. 17**
- **Guzik.** A vivid picture of the ruin waiting for children who mock their parents. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **Clarke.** He ties it back to v. 11 and notes that the disobedient have often died untimely deaths. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-30.html

**vv. 18–20**
- **Guzik.** No advice here, just wonders that should humble us. He reads "she eats" as a tactful way of referring to adultery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **Clarke (citing Holden).** The word "so" ties v. 20 to v. 19: the adulteress hunts like an eagle and winds like a serpent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-30.html
- **Other readings in Clarke.** He notes that some manuscripts and old versions read "a man in his youth." Others take the line as the forming of a child in the womb, or even the virgin birth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-30.html
- **TGC.** Kirk says v. 20 explains the list. A bird, snake or ship leaves no trail, and the adulterer thinks wiping away the evidence clears him. His point: sin is stupid. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/agur-proverbs-30/

**vv. 21–23**
- **Guzik.** The "servant who becomes king" means a man with a slavish, debased mind, not a servant heart like Jesus'. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/

**vv. 24–28**
- **Guzik.** These small creatures were taught by God, not people, and so can we be. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **Matthew Henry.** Do not admire size or strength; judge people by their wisdom and hard work. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_030.cfm
- **TGC.** Kirk says these animals turn their limits into strengths and model humility, in contrast with the strutting creatures of vv. 29–31. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/agur-proverbs-30/

**vv. 29–31**
- **Guzik.** Four examples of majesty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **Clarke.** He asks whether the Hebrew in v. 31 might be a proper name, "King Alkum." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/proverbs-30.html
- **Translation.** The BSB footnote offers "a king against whom there is no rising up." https://www.biblehub.com/app/proverbs-30.htm

**vv. 32–33**
- **Guzik.** Agur warns against self-exaltation after showing humility himself in vv. 1–4. Anger produces strife as surely as churning produces butter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-30/
- **TGC.** Kirk sees v. 32 as the moral of the whole chapter. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/agur-proverbs-30/
